title: FastAPI Background Work, Caching & Rate Limiting: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on offloading work from FastAPI requests (BackgroundTasks, Celery, ARQ), caching responses in Redis with safe invalidation, and protecting endpoints with slowapi or Redis-counter rate limiting.

chapters.title: Background Work and Caching: The Mental Model
points: Request path rule: keep the response fast, so push slow or non-essential work (emails, reports, webhooks) off the request and cache repeated reads
Three tools, three jobs: BackgroundTasks (in-process, fire-and-forget), task queue (separate worker, durable, retryable), cache (Redis store of computed responses)
Rate limiting is a separate guard: it counts requests per key (IP, user, API key) in a time window and rejects the excess with HTTP 429
Redis is the shared backbone: broker/result store for Celery, job queue for ARQ, cache store, and counter store for rate limits
Interview Point: When do you use BackgroundTasks vs a queue? What does 429 mean and which header tells the client when to retry? Why Redis rather than in-process memory for caches and counters?

chapters.title: BackgroundTasks and Its Limits
points: Usage: add a task param `background_tasks: BackgroundTasks`, then call `background_tasks.add_task(fn, arg, kw=val)`; it runs after the response is sent, in the same process
Sync def tasks run in the threadpool; async def tasks run on the event loop, so a blocking call inside an async task freezes the whole server
No durability: a crash, deploy or restart loses pending tasks, since there is no persistence
No retries, no result retrieval, no status tracking, and exceptions after the response are only logged, never seen by the client
Tasks share the web worker's CPU and memory, so heavy or long jobs slow the API; use a queue for anything long, critical or CPU-heavy
Interview Point: Why can an async background task hurt API latency? What happens to queued BackgroundTasks on a restart? Name three signs you have outgrown BackgroundTasks.

chapters.title: Task Queues: Celery vs ARQ
points: Flow: the API enqueues a message to a broker (Redis/RabbitMQ), a separate worker process pops and runs it, and the result goes to a result backend or Redis key
Celery: `@app.task` plus `fn.delay(args)` or `apply_async(countdown=, retry=)`; run with `celery -A proj worker -l info`; sync-first, has beat for schedules, many features, heavier config
ARQ: async-native and Redis-only; define `async def fn(ctx, arg)`, enqueue with `await redis.enqueue_job('fn', arg)`, run `arq module.WorkerSettings`; a good fit for async FastAPI, minimal features
Reliability settings: Celery `acks_late=True`, `autoretry_for=(Exc,)`, `retry_backoff=True`, `max_retries`; ARQ `max_tries` and job_timeout; make tasks idempotent because delivery is at-least-once
Pitfalls: pass IDs not objects (arguments must be serializable), never block the API waiting on `.get()`, and set time limits, concurrency and a visibility timeout longer than the longest task
Interview Point: Celery vs ARQ, how do you choose? What does at-least-once delivery mean for task design? How does a client check job status or result?

chapters.title: Redis Response Caching and Invalidation
points: Cache-aside pattern: build the key, `GET`; on a hit return it; on a miss compute, then `SET key val EX ttl` and return; store JSON-serialized data
Key design: include everything that changes the output (path, query params, user or tenant, version, e.g. `v1:products:list:page=2:user=42`); never cache personalized data under a shared key
Invalidation strategies: TTL expiry (simplest), explicit `DEL` on write, key versioning or prefix bump, and `SCAN MATCH prefix*` for groups (never `KEYS` in production)
Add random jitter to TTLs to avoid mass expiry (avalanche), and use a short lock or request coalescing to stop a stampede when a hot key expires
Cache `HTTP` details: use `Cache-Control` and `ETag` for client caching, cache only GET and successful responses, and delete the key after the DB commit, not before
Interview Point: What are the cache-aside, write-through and write-around patterns? How do you handle stampede and stale data? Why is cache invalidation called one of the hard problems?

chapters.title: Rate Limiting with slowapi and Redis Counters
points: slowapi setup: `limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address, storage_uri='redis://...')`, set `app.state.limiter`, register the `RateLimitExceeded` handler, and decorate routes with `@limiter.limit('5/minute')` (the `request: Request` param is required)
Without a storage_uri, slowapi counts in memory per process, so limits break with multiple workers; point it at Redis to share counts
Fixed window counter: `INCR key`, and on the first hit `EXPIRE key window`; simple but allows a double burst at the window edge. Sliding window (sorted set) or token bucket is smoother
Make the check atomic: use a Lua script or `SET NX EX` plus `INCR`, because a separate INCR and EXPIRE can leave a key with no TTL; return 429 with a `Retry-After` header

Pitfalls: behind a proxy `get_remote_address` sees the proxy IP, so read `X-Forwarded-For` only from a trusted proxy; prefer a user or API-key based key; decide fail-open or fail-closed when Redis is down
Interview Point: Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket? Why does an in-memory limiter fail with several workers? What do you return when a limit is hit?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Background Tasks, Caching, Rate Limiting
points: Pick the tool: BackgroundTasks for quick, loss-tolerant work; Celery or ARQ for durable, retryable, heavy jobs; the cache for repeat reads; the limiter for abuse protection
Commands: `background_tasks.add_task(fn, x)`, `fn.delay(x)`, `celery -A proj worker -l info`, `arq mod.WorkerSettings`, `await redis.enqueue_job('fn', x)`
Cache: `GET key`, then compute and `SET key val EX ttl`; `DEL key` on write; versioned keys; ttl jitter; `SCAN` not `KEYS`
Rate limit: `@limiter.limit('10/minute')` with a Redis storage_uri; `INCR` plus `EXPIRE` atomically; reply 429 with `Retry-After`
Checklist: idempotent tasks, IDs not objects, task time limits, user in the cache key, delete after commit, trusted proxy IP, Redis failure policy
Interview Point: Walk through the life of a request that enqueues a job, reads a cached list, and is rate limited. Which part fails if Redis goes down?
